en: Udāna 2.10 Bhaddiyasutta Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Anupiya in the Mango Grove.
Now on that occasion the Venerable Bhaddiya, the son of Kāḷīgodhā, whether gone to the forest, gone to the foot of a tree, or gone to an empty hut, frequently uttered this inspired utterance:
“Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!”
A number of bhikkhus heard the Venerable Bhaddiya, son of Kāḷīgodhā, repeatedly uttering this inspired exclamation while he had gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut:
“Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!
Having heard it, they thought to themselves:
“Friend, there is no doubt that the Venerable Bhaddiya, son of Kālīgodhā, is living the holy life without delight;

for recollecting the pleasure of sovereignty he formerly enjoyed as a householder, even when gone to the forest, gone to the foot of a tree, or gone to an empty hut, he frequently utters this inspired utterance:
‘Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!’”

Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, the Venerable Bhaddiya, the son of Kāḷīgodhā, whether he has gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, frequently utters this inspired utterance:
‘Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!’”
“Without doubt, venerable sir, the Venerable Bhaddiya, the son of Kāḷīgodhā, leads the holy life without delight.

Recalling that pleasure of sovereignty he formerly enjoyed as a householder, even when gone to the forest, gone to the foot of a tree, or gone to an empty hut, he frequently utters this inspired utterance:
‘Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!’”
Then the Blessed One addressed a certain bhikkhu:
“Come, bhikkhu, address the bhikkhu Bhaddiya in my name, saying:
‘Friend Bhaddiya, the Teacher calls you.’”
“Yes, venerable sir,” that bhikkhu replied to the Blessed One. He then approached the Venerable Bhaddiya, the son of Kāḷīgodhā; having approached, he said to Bhaddiya, the son of Kāḷīgodhā:
“Friend Bhaddiya, the Teacher summons you.
“Very well, friend,” the Venerable Bhaddiya, the son of Kāḷīgodhā, replied to that bhikkhu and went to where [the Blessed One was].
The Blessed One approached him; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As the Venerable Bhaddiya, son of Kāḷīgodhā, was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Is it true, Bhaddiya, that even when you have gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, you frequently utter this inspired exclamation: [text continues]"?
‘Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!
“Yes, Bhante.
“But what benefit, Bhaddiya, do you perceive that you so frequently utter this inspired exclamation when you have gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut?”
‘Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!
[The Blessed One said: “Bhante, formerly when I was a householder exercising kingship, my protection was well-arranged both within the inner palace and without the inner palace;
my protection was well-arranged both within the city and without.”
There was well-arranged protection both within the city and outside the city; there was well-arranged protection both within the countryside and outside the countryside.
Yet, venerable sir, though I was thus protected and guarded, I dwelt afraid, anxious, apprehensive, and terrified.

“But now, Bhante, whether I have gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, I dwell alone—fearless, undismayed, unsuspecting, unafraid, unconcerned, with hair on end, subsisting on what others give, with a mind like that of a deer.
Seeing this purpose, Bhante, when I have gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, I frequently utter this inspired exclamation:
‘Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!’”
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired exclamation:
“He in whose inner self there are no agitations,
who has transcended both ‘thus it was’ and ‘thus it shall be’;”
“The gods do not come to behold him who is thus free from fear, happy,
and sorrowless. Tenth.
The second chapter, the Mucalinda Chapter.
Its summary verse:
Mucalinda, the king, and with the staff.
Sakkāra and the lay follower;
the pregnant woman and the one with an only son;
Suppavāsā and Visākhā.
"Kāḷīgodhāya Bhaddiya."
